items.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price

digest.brief: If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike.

items.title: The absolute best Black Friday deals you can still get
items.excerpt: Black Friday is nearly over, but many of this year’s best deals are still available. You can still find some of the lowest prices we’ve seen in-store and online for video games, wireless earbuds, TVs, robot vacuums, and so much more.

digest.brief: This year’s Black Friday deals have launched in waves over the past several weeks, but now the floodgates have officially opened. As usual, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge. With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years.

items.title: We found 60-odd Black Friday deals we love for $100 or less
items.excerpt: Between holiday travel, gifts, and the rising cost of just about everything, expenses can quickly add up during this time of year.

digest.brief: Between holiday travel, gifts, and the rising cost of just about everything, expenses can quickly add up during this time of year. Thankfully, you don’t have to dip too far into your savings to take advantage of some of the better Black Friday deals we’ve seen.

items.title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
items.excerpt: Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW's ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China's BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.

items.title: The best Black Friday deals you can still get on AirPods, Macs, and other Apple gear
items.excerpt: Black Friday is entering the evening, which means one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch is coming to a close.

digest.brief: Black Friday is one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,749 ($250 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is a new low price.

items.title: The best robot vacuums we’ve tested are up to 60 percent off for Black Friday
items.excerpt: Black Friday is here, and if you want a little help keeping your floors clean this holiday season, now is a great time to pick up a robot vacuum.

digest.brief: Black Friday is here, and if you want a little help keeping your floors clean this holiday season, now is a great time to pick up a robot vacuum. Some of the best models we’ve tested over the last year or two are on sale for up to 60 percent off, whether you’re after a basic robovac for quick cleanups or a more advanced model that vacuums, mops, and practically takes care of itself.

items.title: Sony’s 1000XM4C headphones are a Black Friday bargain at $198
items.excerpt: Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better.

digest.brief: The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up.

items.title: Yooka-Laylee’s free upgrade is skipping Xbox
items.excerpt: Playtronic Games is getting ready to launch Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition as a free update on PlayStation 5, Switch 2, and PC on December 15th.

digest.brief: Unfortunately for Xbox owners, the developer says it “can’t commit to any additional platforms for the foreseeable future.” Others, like John Linneman of Digital Foundry, have countered that Yooka-Laylee and the Impossible Lair: Definitive Edition is ultimately a minor update and pointed out that the Xbox Series X version was already available in native 4K, unlike the PS4 and Switch versions.

items.title: Many of our favorite Blu-ray movies are over 50 percent off for Black Friday
items.excerpt: No shade to those who love their subscription services, but viewing physical movies is a time-honored tradition that shouldn’t go away.

digest.brief: No shade to those who love their subscription services, but viewing physical movies is a time-honored tradition that shouldn’t go away. While standard Blu-ray players that display movies at up to 1080p are fairly inexpensive, 4K Blu-ray counterparts that can show movies in all their 4K HDR glory are significantly pricier (but totally worth it if you’re a movie buff).

items.title: jean couvreur transforms iconic train emergency hammers into bookends, wall hooks, and candlesticks
items.excerpt: to celebrate the 45th anniversary of the TGV, designer jean couvreur composes new objects using iconic parts salvaged from the train.

digest.brief: To celebrate the 45th anniversary of the TGV, SNCF invited designer Jean Couvreur to create new objects from salvaged train parts. By leveraging its formal and functional features, Jean Couvreur conceived three distinct creations: bookends that utilize the tool’s weight, a wall hook incorporating its rounded edges, and a candlestick crafted from its handle.

items.title: The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
items.excerpt: We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday.

digest.brief: Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance.

items.title: Core77 Weekly Roundup (11-23-26 to 11-27-26)
items.excerpt: Here's what we looked at this week: Old-school adjustable-height candleholders , foolishly referred to as "courting candles." An industrial designer with synesthesia reimagines the clock.

items.title: Researchers Figure Out How to Turn Your Arm Into a Smartwatch Trackpad
items.excerpt: Smartwatches are a convenient way to display small pieces of information. However, their tiny screens make for lousy input devices.

digest.brief: Smartwatches are a convenient way to display small pieces of information. "Smartwatch screens are too small for the touch interactions people use every day on phones and laptops," says Chenhan Xu, an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at North Carolina State University, "such as two-finger scrolling, pinch-to-zoom, or pressing harder to trigger a different command."

items.title: pliavo’s portable piano folds 84 keys accordion-style into a compact block
items.excerpt: an accordion-like system of hinges allows musicians to compress an entire seven-octave keyboard into a block just over 6 inches long.

digest.brief: Denver-based Pliavo introduces its Fold-and-Go Piano, a portable digital instrument whose 84 keys collapse into a compact bundle small enough to carry inside a backpack. While many compact electronic pianos take the form of flexible silicone mats, here the musician plays across a continuous arrangement of rigid keys with three millimeters of vertical travel.

items.title: aluminum composite shell and bamboo interior define lavvu mobile home unit in armenia
items.excerpt: lavvu introduces a transportable modular home that combines automotive-inspired engineering, panoramic glazing and a carefully crafted interior to create a more flexible way of living close to nature.

digest.brief: Developed and manufactured in Armenia by Re:Büro, LAVVU XL is a transportable modular dwelling that applies automotive manufacturing principles to residential architecture. At the core of the module is a welded steel frame paired with lightweight internal framing, mineral wool insulation, and an aluminum composite exterior shell.

items.title: Usability Testing 101
items.excerpt: Usability testing involves watching people use a design to uncover problems and opportunities. Anyone on a product team can learn this. Usability testing (sometimes called user testing ) is a popular UX-research method.

digest.brief: Summary: Usability testing involves watching people use a design to uncover problems and opportunities. Usability testing is a research method in which researchers observe people attempting a realistic task with one or more user interfaces, to identify usability problems and opportunities for improvement.

MIT Technology Review identified more than a dozen cases involving high-end vehicles, obtained court records, and spoke to law enforcement, brokers, drivers, and victims in multiple states to reveal how transport fraud is wreaking havoc across the country.

items.title: a review of midcentury kinetic environments: when artists turned entire rooms into moving machines
items.excerpt: in the 1960s, artists began using motors, elastic structures, and pneumatic systems to transform the spaces we inhabit. The post a review of midcentury kinetic environments: when artists turned entire rooms into moving machines appeared first on designboom | architecture & design magazine .

digest.brief: Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, an international network of artists began to explore the possibilities of kinetic art at the scale of architecture. Over the following decade, some of the most ambitious projects in kinetic art would take the form of environments that visitors could physically enter. Schöffer also developed an animated light wall for the neighboring building.

items.title: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.excerpt: Next up in our 20/20 project marking 20 years of Dezeen is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.

digest.brief: Next up in Dezeen's 20x20 project in partnership with Kohler, which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship. Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer Wearstler, who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.

items.title: Liminal
items.excerpt: Far from home, injured Ukrainians soldiers learn how to be in their bodies once again, and how to inhabit the world - Directed by Brennan Vance Watch on Psyche.

digest.brief: At the Protez Foundation in Oakdale, Minnesota, such patients are fitted with state-of-the-art prosthetics free of charge and are taught how to use their new limbs. For the film, the director Brennan Vance profiled a group of Ukrainian soldiers who, injured on the front lines, came to Minnesota to recover far from the brutal war that had defined their lives for years.

items.title: singapore’s artscience museum shows design beyond the human realm
items.excerpt: discover how design goes beyond humans to include animals and ecosystems as active collaborators in this expanded exhibition The post singapore’s artscience museum shows design beyond the human realm appeared first on designboom | architecture & design magazine .

digest.brief: From November 28, 2026, to May 16, 2027, visitors can experience More than Human: Making With the Living World at ArtScience Museum. Building on the original London presentation, the Singapore edition has been significantly expanded and co-curated by ArtScience Museum and the Design Museum, London, with support from the DesignSingapore Council.

items.title: The energy of thought
items.excerpt: We have an astonishing number of models of how the mind works. All of them neglect something essential - by David Colaço & Philipp Haueis Read on Aeon.

digest.brief: Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta, Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply.

items.title: Fairuz in the morning and Umm Kulthum at night
items.excerpt: Back home in Palestine, my grandparents’ music drove me mad. Now I’m in the US, I’m the one singing along - by Elissa Odeh Read on Psyche.

digest.brief: After playing in their yard until sunset, my cousins and I would gather on their bed, where Teta would turn down Umm Kulthum on the television to tell us the story of the Elderly Woman and her Cow while slicing apples. Eyes half-open, I put on my school uniform and ran down the stairs to my grandparents’ house, the scent of Arabic coffee rising from the stove.

digest.brief: Every year, the editors at MIT Technology Review select 35 of the world’s top young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors to honor as our newest class of Innovators Under 35. items.excerpt: Plus: what's behind the current trend for food-oriented streetwear? And what's wrong with Snøhetta's amazing new Shanghai Grand Opera House? The post The debate over putting trees on buildings appeared first on Dezeen .

digest.brief: Listen to the latest episode of Dezeen Weekly now. In this week's episode, Jennifer Hahn and Nat Barker dive into the debate surrounding one of 21st-century architecture's major movements: buildings festooned with trees. The post The debate over putting trees on buildings appeared first on Dezeen.

items.title: How cutting-edge prosthetics can help probe the human mind
items.excerpt: Avi Davidson has volunteered to find out how a bionic hand that feels might alter his brain and nervous system. Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson.

digest.brief: Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi’s arm. What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job.

items.title: 1960s grand touring car design shapes acte deux’s paris apartment renovation
items.excerpt: inspired by automotive interiors and streamlined bodywork, the 65-square-meter renovation combines lacquered surfaces, polished metal and warm timber to rethink domestic space.

digest.brief: Acte Deux, founded by Johanna Lapray and Hugo L’ahélec, renovates a 65-square-meter apartment in the Paris’s 18th arrondissement, drawing on the streamlined forms and richly appointed interiors of 1960s grand touring cars. Paris-based design studio Acte Deux reorganizes the living spaces into a continuous horizontal sequence.

items.title: Rachel Whiteread punctures 2027 Brit Award trophy
items.excerpt: Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year's Brit Awards trophy, a silver statuette covered in holes to "expose the interior of the statue".

digest.brief: Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year's Brit Awards trophy, a silver sculpture covered in holes to "expose the interior of the statue". Essex-born Whiteread has designed the statuette for next February's ceremony, which is her interpretation of the annual trophy depicting Britannia, a helmeted warrior that is a traditional symbol of Britain.

items.title: Worn into shape
items.excerpt: A pebble acquires its shape through contact: with water, with grit, with other stones. The objects gathered here bring that familiarity into manufactured form.

digest.brief: A pebble acquires its shape through contact: with water, with grit, with other stones. The objects gathered here bring that familiarity into manufactured form, from things carried in a pocket to a place to sit. New case files, exhibitions, and interviews, delivered to your inbox.

items.title: The year the web industry gave up
items.excerpt: The one where I lament what the web industry once was. I’ve been drafting my personal “year in review” and one topic stood out as needing its own follow-up. So let’s get that out of the way! That’s sarcasm.

digest.brief: Nevertheless, today I’m talking about/to the real web industry. TL;DR: the web industry is dismantling itself from the inside. People who have spent years, decades in some cases, building a reputation as leaders within the web industry are now destroying what they’ve built.

items.title: I’m a 100x engineer now
items.excerpt: Extremely enthusiastic and about 100x faster with AI. It has changed my entire workflow, and my life. (This essay won second prize (and $2,500! 🎉) in The Pragmatic Engineer ’s essay challenge ).

digest.brief: 194 sweaty, reviewed, production-ready code lines from my own little fingers—okay, with the help of GitHub Copilot. Over the last 10 months, I also built Prvw, a simple and delightful free image viewer (135k LoC), a few libraries that support Cmdr (mtp-rs being 45k LoC and smb2 116k LoC), plus several side projects like gitstrata.

items.title: Design.md VS Code Extension
items.excerpt: A VS Code extension that adds linting, autocomplete and a rich preview for design.md design system files. I’ve been working a lot with DESIGN.md files recently.

digest.brief: Broken token references, missing primary colors, low contrast, unused tokens and out-of-order sections show up in the Problems panel as you type. Front matter checks for a missing or empty name and duplicate keys, each flagged on the exact line. Rich preview with color swatches, typography samples, spacing and radius scales, component previews, the rendered prose and the lint results.

items.title: Vladimir Nabokov on What Makes a Good Reader
items.excerpt: "A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader." Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going.

digest.brief: “All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,” H. Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life. The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.

items.title: rounded volumes and sweet color palettes shape dessert-inspired lighting collection
items.excerpt: what if a lamp could be as tempting as your favorite dessert? decadent studio presents chubby, a collection of table lamps inspired by the shapes, colors and textures of sweet treats.

digest.brief: Chubby is the first lighting collection by Decadent Studio, an independent design studio based in Galicia, Spain. Inspired by desserts such as pavlova, cherry pie and tangerine ice cream, the collection explores the relationship between food, design and desire. Decadent Studio pays special attention to every detail, from the color of the textile cable to the back of the lamp.

items.title: A Vintage Lighting Design Classic: Carlo Nason's Sfumato Floor Lamp
items.excerpt: In 1966 Carlo Nason, an Italian glassmaker and self-taught designer, created this LT316 Lamp. Designed for manufacturer Mazzega, the lamp consisted of hand-blown glass sections that stacked, with one section per lightbulb.

digest.brief: In 1966 Carlo Nason, an Italian glassmaker and self-taught designer, created this LT316 Lamp. Designed for manufacturer Mazzega, the lamp consisted of hand-blown glass sections that stacked, with one section per lightbulb. Had 2001: A Space Odyssey come out earlier than it did (1968), you get the feeling this lamp would have appeared in it.

items.title: charred wooden modules conceal six-sided mirror chamber inside interactive play installation
items.excerpt: alchemy is a two-module free-play installation that guides children and adults through dark inflatable chambers, a six-sided mirror room, and a pink recycled foam space.

digest.brief: Designed by Florian López, Alchemy is an interactive free-play installation for children and adults that organizes an exhibition space as an anatomical body to be traversed. The post charred wooden modules conceal six-sided mirror chamber inside interactive play installation appeared first on designboom | architecture & design magazine.

items.title: sinuous stone-roofed visitor center meanders through the mountains of china
items.excerpt: a river's movement informs the geometry of two visitor centers, where sweeping roofs choreograph pedestrian journeys through the mountains.

digest.brief: The Huangguoshu Scenic Area in China‘s mountainous Guizhou province welcomes visitors beneath a pair of serpentine roofs designed by the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design (CAUPD) and AEPA&TSC. At the Great Waterfall visitor center, the design team takes advantage of an existing five-meter difference in elevation between the entrance and exit of the scenic area.

items.title: Five lighting designs listed by Marset on Dezeen Showroom
items.excerpt: Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.

digest.brief: Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice. Marset's selection includes the Gambosa table lamp, created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

items.title: Royal Society for Arts appoints five Royal Designers for Industry
items.excerpt: The UK's Royal Society for Arts has announced the five Royal Designers for Industry thand named an Honorary Royal Designer. The post Royal Society for Arts appoints five Royal Designers for Industry appeared first on Dezeen .

digest.brief: The UK's Royal Society for Arts has announced five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary. Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.

items.title: Base Design gives Visa a brand refresh "for the next generation"
items.excerpt: As part of a visual identity update for Visa, design agency Base Design created a more "compact" version of its logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a new typeface.

digest.brief: Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card company Visa's logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a new typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand's visual identity. "When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn't recognition – it's relevance," said Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

items.title: The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love
items.excerpt: "Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment."

digest.brief: “The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on why we fall and how we stay in love. Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical.

items.title: concrete, lime-washed brick, and color-blocked zones organize movebon boutique training studio
items.excerpt: designed by jotajota+, movebon is a 126-sqm boutique training studio organized around an elliptical tubular lighting fixture, a concrete block focal wall, color-blocked zones, and custom galvanized steel and timber storage units.

digest.brief: Occupying 126 sqm, Movebon is a boutique training studio in Madrid designed by JOTAJOTA+ around a clear spatial division between an open workout area and private service facilities. In the main workout space, both the floor and ceiling are coated in brown-red (RAL 3011), framing sightlines toward a newly built concrete block wall at the rear.

items.title: Lighting that feels just right
items.excerpt: An explainer and personal experience learning and leveraging screen-space and probe-based Global Illumination rendering methods. In The Gap , Ira Glass talks about the frustration of your output falling short of what you originally envisioned when learning a new skill.

digest.brief: A brightly lit surface contributes no lighting at all to the objects or scene around it. In our Volumetric Lighting work, we had to reconstruct a surface’s position to know when to stop marching a ray from the camera 5. A surface can receive light from many directions, so we can’t just trace a single ray and hope to get a reliable estimate of its indirect lighting.

items.title: 12ft Lab
items.excerpt: Experiments, tools and prototypes from 12ft. Experiments and prototypes that come about alongside our client work, kept because we find them fun or useful.

digest.brief: This is where we collect the experiments, tools and prototypes that come about alongside our projects at 12ft. Experiments and prototypes that come about alongside our client work, kept because we find them fun or useful. Tools we build to make our lives simpler, and hopefully yours too.

items.title: High fidelity, low definition
items.excerpt: Form clarity through deliberate design fidelity. In the beginning of my career I worked as an identity designer. Gradually I moved into digital products as a "visual designer," where I worked alongside an information architect that would spec out wireframes.

digest.brief: Later, when the industry collapsed both roles into the "product designer," I still found it common to move from low to high fidelity in many of my projects. Now I am seeing a pattern on AI-native teams: they start in high fidelity prototypes. Low fidelity enables your team to move at high velocity in the stages of early definition.

items.title: Forward-deployed design as plumbing
items.excerpt: Notes on forward-deployed design, coordination debt and two classroom builds of scoped public fixes. I'm revisiting the forward-deployed design discussion, and I think the shape of teams is less important to me.

digest.brief: The product designer was closer to the designer-engineer archetype that’s always existed in some orgs, but AI is upending this and making everyone feel some need to rebrand into some kind of engineer to stay semirelevant in these complicated times. The whole “Design as Repair” ethos was really about what I told friends: designers as the folks who get into coveralls and tackle the problem.

items.title: Tegaki
items.excerpt: Open-source handwriting animation library and generator: any font, written stroke by stroke in natural stroke order. An open-source handwriting animation library for any font.

digest.brief: Tegaki extracts each glyph's strokes, their order and width, and draws them stroke by stroke on a canvas over real, selectable text. Hebrew and Arabic right to left with positional forms, Devanagari and Bengali headlines drawn across the word, and Japanese, Korean and Chinese in reference stroke order (KanjiVG, Make Me a Hanzi).

items.title: Lina Ghotmeh: archaeology of the future
items.excerpt: In the work of the Lebanese architect Lina Ghotmeh, the scars of the past inform resilient buildings for the future - by Aeon Video Watch on Aeon.

digest.brief: The Lebanese architect Lina Ghotmeh is known for works that preserve memories of the past but are built for the future. This short documentary from the London-based director Stephen Pook deconstructs Ghotmeh’s approach to architecture, revealing how her designs and thoughtful use of materials are born of a process in which history matters as much as the physical environment.

items.title: The pretendian wars
items.excerpt: To falsely claim Indigenous identity is not a frivolous mistake. It’s a grave theft, and the stakes are getting higher - by Dina Gilio-Whitaker Read on Aeon.

digest.brief: Anthropologists who study Indigenous cultural identity use the term ethnogenesis to describe how the identities of ethnic communities are formed or understood, and how they can change over time. People ‘become’ Indian when they claim to ‘be’ Indian with no connection to a tribal community, or little to no evidence of Native ancestry.

items.title: What exile was like for the first people called ‘refugees’
items.excerpt: Persecuted in 17th-century France, the Huguenots fled their homeland. Their memoirs reveal how they suffered and survived - by Nora Baker Read on Psyche.

digest.brief: One dark night in 1683, a 19-year-old girl from the small town of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, not far from Grenoble in southeastern France, approached the fire in the hearth of her family home. This was a time of high religious tension in France, and Blanche Gamond’s Protestant family had been forced to host soldiers in their house whose goal it was to intimidate them into converting to Catholicism.

items.title: There and back
items.excerpt: A lost home lives on in spikes of joy and longing; it shifts in memory as life changes. But it’s never the same - by Pam Weintraub Read on Psyche.

digest.brief: At first, our cluster of 19 buildings in an East New York housing project had felt like a little town; we walked safely everywhere, just us kids. In our new ‘luxe digs’ in Co-op City in the Bronx, I carried the world that made me: the asphalt park called the Circle, where I raced on roller skates tightened by key; nights on concrete barrels, transistor radios straining with Stevie Wonder and the early Stones.

items.title: "How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"
items.excerpt: In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it's possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

digest.brief: In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it's possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan. During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

items.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

Keeping the mark simple paid off right away when we got to color. Where we landed keeps a thread back to Copilot’s original gradient while letting color shift and blend from one context to the next.

items.title: What It Takes to Build Great Products Now

For example, if there’s too much space between a form field and a button, it may be quicker to adjust the spacing directly in Figma than to describe the change in a prompt. From visual editing to contextual prompting and collaboration, Figma Make is expanding how teams can design with code.

items.title: Create Ways of Being

digest.brief: Almost overnight, we went from simply using mobile phones to living almost entirely in a digital world. Before I turned twenty, I loved sitting by the pond beneath an apricot tree on campus. Inspired by these ideas, I wanted my art to create space for people to perceive more deeply, become present, and imagine other ways of being.

items.title: Bringing Emoji into the Next Era of Expression
items.excerpt: The unexpected design challenges of translating 2D emoji into open-source 3D. In a live chat, ending a sentence with a period reads like an act of aggression. That’s just the emotional tax of talking through glass.

digest.brief: While every emoji was shaped by human hands, ensuring that emotional clarity could scale across thousands of screens required an assist from automation. In dark mode, people who use darker skin tones have long faced an annoying reality: Their emoji often disappear against black or dark-gray chat bubbles.

items.title: Google named Fast Company’s Design Company of the Year
items.excerpt: Google is Fast Company’s Design Company of the Year. A look at how our design teams are translating breakthrough AI into everyday, intuitive experiences.

digest.brief: Fast Company has recognized Google as its 2026 Design Company of the Year in the annual Innovation by Design Awards—honoring our collective effort to transform our products and experiences with AI. Search AI Mode, which reimagines information discovery, organizing complex, nuanced, and multimodal queries into clear, explorative journeys.

items.title: AI, tools and transformation
items.excerpt: It’s very tempting to imagine that AI turns everyone into a tool-builder - now everyone can just ask the model to make the software they need, and apps as we know them are dead.

digest.brief: Your users, bottom-up and creating their own solutions, manage these in a fuzzy, improvised space of freeform substrates like Excel, email, shared folders, Tableau, Powerpoint and CSVs, screenshots, PDFs and conference calls. All of those SaaS apps do something that you could do in SAP or Excel or email - Carta is a $4bn company that manages one spreadsheet for your CFO - and sometimes tasks move back.

items.title: How Coinbase Used Code Connect to Guide Agents and Shrink Token Costs
items.excerpt: The Coinbase Design System team put Code Connect to the test against coding agents—and found that it boosted design system adherence while cutting token costs by an average of 22.

digest.brief: With Code Connect in Figma’s MCP, they get that context. “Based on what I’d heard about Code Connect, it was a way to improve the reliability of design-to-code workflows without having to rely solely on our agent skills,” says Erich. Code Connect is part of every component workflow on the CDS engineering team.

items.title: Behind the Build: Generative Plugins and Shaders at Figma
items.excerpt: Starting today, you’ll have more creative control over generative plugins and shaders, and a way to share what you’ve made with the community.

digest.brief: Community and internal publishing: Publish plugins and shaders that you’ve created with the Figma design agent to the Figma Community, or privately to your organization if you’re on an Organization or Enterprise plan. Georgia encouraged us to combine forces under the umbrella of generative tools: a suite of ways to use agents on the canvas to create custom plugins and shaders on the fly.

items.title: How Do You Actually Measure the Impact of AI on Design?
items.excerpt: In 2024, we kicked off a study to understand how AI would reshape design and product development. Now, AI is helping us run it.

digest.brief: When AI tools and products started gaining momentum a few years ago, we knew we wanted to track their impact on the design industry, from ways of working to product development strategy. To build Figma’s AI impact index, we asked designers, developers, and PMs questions like “Over the past 12 months, to what degree has AI affected your personal productivity and workflows?”

items.title: Workflow Lab: Moving Between Design and Code With Agents
items.excerpt: Coding agents are reshaping how developers build, but they’re only as good as the input they’re given. This workflow explores how context keeps code and canvas in sync.

digest.brief: Given more design context to work from—like approved components and tokens documented in Figma—a coding agent can match your intent in fewer prompts. In this example workflow, a developer at Radicle uses Figma dev tools to give their coding agent better context so it can generate better code. , which gives the agent access to the components, tokens, and layouts in Radicle’s design system.

items.title: How To Move Fast Toward the Right Thing
items.excerpt: With AI, speed comes easy, but so does tech debt. That’s why the best teams don’t just ship something fast; they consider it carefully, build it efficiently, and make it stand out.

digest.brief: For most of software history, code was the gate to product building, and developers held the keys. Product development teams feel the pressure to keep executing and accelerating, but that speed can cloud our judgment—we can mistake polished outputs for good ones. A recent white paper from Google on agentic coding describes how low-effort vibe coding leads to tech debt.

items.title: Code is a Design Material
items.excerpt: A designer’s reflections from Config, and why UX fundamentals matter more than ever. Katie Jacquez is a Senior UX Designer working on the next generation of merchant tools and consumer experiences for the Google Store.

digest.brief: AI-driven tools grant us an undeniable superpower: the ability to spin up high-fidelity prototypes faster than we could previously imagine. On a recent project building an internal tool for the Google store, I used AI to generate an early prototype, which was exactly what we needed to align on the core workflow, draft the PRD, and shape our product strategy.

items.title: Ways to think about token pricing
items.excerpt: AI is in a supply crunch today, but what happens when we come out of it? How and where will supply, demand, price, capacity and capex get back into equilibrium?

digest.brief: All of the variables are in play, and the market will get shaken out over the next few years to arrive at a new equilibrium. Right now we have a lot of frantic analysis of ‘time to power’, but the question at the end of that remains whether the foundation models have sustainable pricing power, strategic leverage and value capture, or whether they become low-margin commodity infrastructure providers.

items.title: It's time to tame the monsters of healthcare
items.excerpt: How health organizations can overcome obstacles to improve outcomes. In our healthcare work, we’re constantly partnering with clients to solve big, seemingly intractable problems that prevent them from delivering the care patients need.

digest.brief: In our healthcare work, we’re constantly partnering with clients to solve big, seemingly intractable problems that prevent them from delivering the care patients need. Over the decades, we’ve learned it’s easier to tame these monsters if you name them. Taming this monster starts with a question that isn’t asked often enough in healthcare: “Does it need to feel like this?”

items.title: Predicting AI job exposure
items.excerpt: Many people would like to analyse which jobs, companies and industries are most exposed to AI, and assign scores, build charts, and map that against the progress of LLMs.

digest.brief: Indeed, if you dig into the detail of the Census data, then ‘accountants and auditors’ itself is a fairly stable category, but all around that term there are lots of other finance job categories that appear and disappear over time. The job of “Billing, posting and calculating machine operator” appeared in the stats for a decade or so and then disappeared again.

items.title: The AI dividend
items.excerpt: The case for investing in the creative frontier. “The smarter move is to think of efficiency not as the destination, but as the mechanism that creates room for something far more valuable."

digest.brief: The surplus of human bandwidth, creative energy, and organizational capacity that automation liberates. The AI Dividend should be invested in a new, more nimble and dynamic organization at the creative frontier: exploring the unmeasured territory where AI models cannot yet operate and where human sensibility, intuition, and judgment create genuine differentiation.

items.title: How will OpenAI compete?
items.excerpt: OpenAI has some big questions. It doesn’t have unique tech. It has a big user base, but with limited engagement and stickiness and no network effect.

digest.brief: Nor does OpenAI have consumer products on top of the models themselves that have product-market fit. Big aggressive incumbents and thousands of entrepreneurs are trying to create new features, experiences and business models, and in the process try to turn foundation models themselves into commodity infrastructure sold at marginal cost.

items.title: Illustrating the Gemini App
items.excerpt: How dynamic cues help users discover, learn, and master our AI assistant’s evolving features. How do you build trust in a tool that’s always evolving?

digest.brief: In this deep dive, the designers behind the system pull back the curtain to reveal gradients, responsive containers, and intentional motion that seamlessly work together to create a sense of magic, clarity, and familiarity within the Gemini experience. Gradients are central to Gemini’s visual storytelling, acting as context builders that guide users through the product experience.

items.title: Making Google Sans Flex
items.excerpt: How seven design problems shaped Google’s iconic typeface — from inception to going open source. Sometimes, design elements are birthed in flashes of inspiration — What if our interfaces were like paper ?

digest.brief: When Google Sans rolled out in 2018, designers were initially ecstatic. “But it also created a dual-font system using Google Sans for larger display text and Roboto for smaller text. Google Sans Text rolled out on the Pixel 3, creating a more unified typographic experience.

items.title: AI, networks and Mechanical Turks
items.excerpt: How far do LLMs give us a step change in how good a search and recommendation system can be? Do they let you build one without needing a vast user base of your own?

digest.brief: Any consumer internet system with critical mass becomes, in part, a Mechanical Turk. Amazon knows that if you bought X, you might buy Y, because it's seen what lots of people buy and saw that if they buy X, they're likely to buy Y. Amazon has close to a billion SKUs, but all it knows about them is the metadata typed in by humans and some level of purchase correlation.

items.title: Read smarter, not harder, with Lumi
items.excerpt: Lumi UX concept As research engineers, our reading lists are always exciting… and also way too long to finish. While we’d love to go through every research paper at a leisurely, note-taking pace, the reality of the work week means that we end up skimming the abstract, scrolling quickly through sections and diagrams, and, more often than not, missing interesting points along the way.

digest.brief: While we’d love to go through every research paper at a leisurely, note-taking pace, the reality of the work week means that we end up skimming the abstract, scrolling quickly through sections and diagrams, and, more often than not, missing interesting points along the way. Our prototype, Lumi, is an interface for arXiv papers that incorporates AI as a lightweight layer on top of the source material.

items.title: True Design Is Better Than New Design

digest.brief: David Reinfurt discusses how individual perspective is the real driver of a design practice. Designer, educator, and author David Reinfurt returns to Design Notes to discuss his latest book, A *Co-* Program for Graphic Design. Reinfurt discusses the power of hands-on learning, the importance of going against expectations, and how closely design exists to everyday life.

items.title: Unboxing a New Collaboration
items.excerpt: If hardware and software can work together, so can their teams. When you unbox a new Pixel Phone or Watch this year, you’ll be holding the results of the new collaborative standard set by a group of Google designers from two very different design fields – industrial and interface.

digest.brief: When you unbox a new Pixel Phone or Watch this year, you’ll be holding the results of the new collaborative standard set by a group of Google designers from two very different design fields – industrial and interface. Interface designers work on the software inside those objects to make them useful in the digital space.

items.title: UX Design as Dance Theater
items.excerpt: Just like dance, great product design thrives on iteration, collaboration, and attention to detail. Euphrates Dahout is a Google UX Designer and the architect of the world’s most popular Figma library, the M3 Design Kit .

digest.brief: Euphrates Dahout is a Google UX Designer and the architect of the world’s most popular Figma library, the M3 Design Kit. The process of designing a digital experience mirrors that of choreographing a performance: It requires vision, iteration, and meticulous attention to detail. Hitting the right beat in a dance routine is akin to maintaining accuracy in design systems.

items.title: When Brand Fonts are Open Source
items.excerpt: Discover why brands from IBM to Github open up their fonts to everyone, and how you can reap the rewards. Reddit, IBM, and the Finnish government have probably never been listed in the same sentence before.

digest.brief: Discover why brands from IBM to Github open up their fonts to everyone, and how you can reap the rewards. Google’s own font superfamily, Noto, was developed as a set of fonts for all languages—a major feat considering the vast differences in how text appears in different writing systems. If anyone knows the value of open source, it’s GitHub, so of course their custom fonts Mona Sans and Hubot Sans are on fonts.

items.title: Inside M3 Expressive
items.excerpt: Go behind the scenes with product, research, and design. Design Notes is a podcast by Liam Spradlin about creative work and what it teaches us.

digest.brief: Go behind the scenes with product, research, and design. This very special episode digs into the latest evolution of Google’s design system: Material 3 Expressive. Liam talks with Material Design’s Android Product Manager Aneesha Kommineni, UX Researcher Michael Gilbert, and Creative Director Andy Stewart about the team’s latest emotion-driven UX update.

items.title: AI metrics
items.excerpt: With every platform shift, we want to measure the growth but we’re confused about what to measure. That’s partly a problem of data and definitions, but it’s really a question about what this is going to be.

digest.brief: In the early days of the consumer Internet, a lot of metrics floated around and no-one was clear what to measure or what it meant. Usage and users are growing, yes, but meanwhile the models have become far more efficient on one hand and on the other agents and media creation use far more tokens for a given request, and of course Google is showing ‘AI Overviews’ to everyone.

items.title: GenAI’s adoption puzzle
items.excerpt: Generative AI chatbots might be a life-changing transformation in the nature of computing, that can replace all software, but so far, most of its users only pick it up every week or two, and far fewer have made it part of their lives.

digest.brief: In a sense that’s a skewed comparison - ChatGPT is just a website, it gets wall-to-wall media coverage (this is part of Sam Altman’s job), and you don’t need to buy a thousand dollar device or wait for telcos to deploy broadband. Sam Altman knows this - he was trying to build a social media app at the time, and yet the traction number he always gives is, well, ‘weekly active users’.

items.title: Opportunities in the hidden costs of caregiving
items.excerpt: Hard-won lessons from a designer supporting her father. As my father and I prepared to head to Stanford for yet another doctor’s appointment, I remember asking him, “Are you prepared to never walk again?”

digest.brief: At 22, I came face-to-face with the hidden costs of healthcare when my father became paraplegic. As both a caregiver and a designer, I deeply understand these pain points and how we can design solutions that ease the burden on the 24 million caregivers in the US alone—whether it’s creating clear, comprehensible medical bills or developing devices that help prevent further health complications.

items.title: What kind of disruption?
items.excerpt: Software ate the world. Uber and Airbnb didn’t sell software - they disrupted and redefined markets. But what kind of disruption are we talking about ?

digest.brief: Everyone knows about ‘disruption’, and it’s pretty common also to talk about redefining markets and ‘software eating the world’, and Airbnb and Uber are the perfect examples. Where previous generations of tech companies sold software to hotels and taxi companies, Airbnb and Uber used software to create new businesses and to redefine markets.

items.title: Apple innovation and execution
items.excerpt: It matters that Apple’s new Siri will be late, and it matters more that Apple didn’t realise. Is it more than that? People have been claiming that Apple has forgotten how to innovate since the early 1980s, or longer - it’s a standing joke in talking about the company.

digest.brief: Apple changed the world with the Mac and the iPhone, but the iPhone will be old enough to vote this summer, and, as the saying goes, ‘what have you done for us lately?’ The iPad is a little polarising amongst tech people (and it remains unfinished business, as Apple concedes in how often it fiddles with the keyboard and the multitasking) but after a rocky start it’s stabilised as roughly the same size as the Mac.

items.title: The Deep Research problem
items.excerpt: OpenAI’s Deep Research is built for me, and I can’t use it. It’s another amazing demo, until it breaks. But it breaks in really interesting ways.

digest.brief: Deep Research says that the Japanese smartphone market is split 69% iOS and 31% Android. If we check Statista, we have to jump through a bunch of hoops, but eventually find that the actual source is the research firm Kantar Worldpanel, and the numbers it gives are pretty much the exact opposite of what Deep Research claims - 63% Android and 36% iOS.

items.title: Are better models better?
items.excerpt: Every week there’s a better AI model that gives better answers. But a lot of questions don’t have better answers, only ‘right’ answers, and these models can’t do that.

digest.brief: Hence, the two fields where generative AI has clear, early and strong product-market fit are software development and marketing: mistakes are generally easy to see (or test for) and there aren’t necessarily wrong answers. If I ask for a few hundred words of copy about a new product or brand, there might not be a ‘wrong’ answer, and if it’s your product then you can spot the mistakes - this is still hugely useful.

items.title: Scaling Training Data Attribution
items.excerpt: The science of how training data influences LLM behavior Written by Tyler A. Chang , with Dheeraj Rajagopal , Tolga Bolukbasi , Lucas Dixon , and Ian Tenney .

digest.brief: One promising branch of methods to understanding this process is called training data attribution (TDA). In our paper, “Scalable Influence and Fact Tracing for Large Language Model Pretraining”, we demonstrate how training data attribution methods can scale to LLM pretraining. TrackStar takes a model prediction and ranks training examples by their estimated influence on that prediction.

items.title: Falling in Love with Generated Images
items.excerpt: by Adam Connors and Grady Simon The AI-Augmented life project aims to explore the ways that AI might change our everyday lives. So when my colleague mentioned that he’d been using generated imagery for day-to-day communication with his partner since July 2022, I had to learn more.

digest.brief: For him, generated images fulfill a unique role in his interactions with his partner — they’re more expressive than emojis, more personal than memes. Grady is living the future of generated imagery, persevering with an emerging technology that still contains lots of friction points, because the generated images add something new and important to the way he communicates.

items.title: Model Alignment Through Automatic Prompt Updates From User Feedback
items.excerpt: by James Wexler (PAIR Software Engineer) and Colby Hawker (Vertex AI Product Manager) TL:DR; Creating a prompt that accurately captures a prompt developer’s intent can be a complex and challenging task.

digest.brief: A significant advantage with this alignment approach is that it only requires critiquing a model response to a prompt in plain language, and doesn’t require a large predefined set of “ground truth” labeled examples. The developer can co-develop their prompt with a language model in an iterative loop by providing feedback and testing the corresponding prompt updates.

items.title: Building the AI-Augmented Life

items.title: Talking to My AI (Part #1) — Exploring the surprisingly useful illusion of human-like conversation
items.excerpt: Talking to My AI (Part #1) — Exploring the surprisingly useful illusion of human-like conversation by Adam Connors The AI-Augmented life project is exploring ways that AI might change our everyday lives in the coming years.

digest.brief: Humans love interacting with other humans, and in the moments when the illusion flickers into life — when the AI meets my unspoken expectations — I find myself leaning forward, engaging more deeply than I would have if I were typing. When the illusion of a human-like interaction flickers into life, my engagement (my ability to think) rises.

items.title: Talking to My AI (Part #2) — Is it useful yet?

With my son safely packed off to school, I started to wonder if talking to a voice-powered AI assistant might be a better way to learn something complex like this than reading articles or having a text-based conversation with a chatbot.

items.title: “Teach my son History” — How I used AI to help my son remember stuff
items.excerpt: “Teach my son History” — How I used AI to help my son remember stuff A week before his final exams and this is what my son’s bedroom floor looks like: My son’s bedroom floor a month before his final exams.

digest.brief: Each card covers a different aspect of the syllabus, and we use them to come up with questions that we grill our son with. The most important moments are when my son gives an incomplete or almost correct answer. Secondly, the system must build a model of what the student knows, and provide hints in order to ensure that the student takes an active role in filling in any gaps.

items.title: Competing in search
items.excerpt: A quarter century after ‘don't be evil’ a judge has found that Google is abusing its monopoly in search. But no-one knows what happens next, and whether this ruling will change anything. Will Apple build a search engine?

digest.brief: A search engine is a vast mechanical Turk - a reinforcement learning engine that uses human activity to understand the web. 50% of search in the USA happens on channels where Google has a contract to make it the default: 28% on Apple devices, 19. A lot of people given a choice screen would just choose Google anyway, as indeed appears to have happened in the EU, which already mandated this on Android.

items.title: Building the plane while flying it: an LLM case study
items.excerpt: By Quinn Madison, Alexa Koenings, Iris Chu, Pratheek I, from Google Dev AI UX, with contributions from Laurie Pham, Google Dev AI UX Enable user feedback, design for steerability, set expectations so users can calibrate their trust in your AI system.

digest.brief: The tool, a proprietary LLM related to Google’s Gemini models, was trained on a corpus of internal SWE data and over time, enabled developers to code faster and get answers quickly to technical questions in their day-to-day work. Develocity illustrates how generative AI models — specifically, LLMs capable of writing code — might enable developers to write, test, share, and manage code across their workflows.
